lesson.title: Running Out of Rail
lesson.summary: An op-amp's output can only swing within its supply voltages, so any signal that the ideal closed-loop gain equation predicts to exceed those rails instead flattens out, or saturates, close to the supply rail.
lesson.body:
Every closed-loop gain equation used so far, Vout = Gain x Vin, quietly assumes the op-amp's output can move to whatever voltage the math demands. A real op-amp is powered from a finite voltage source, the supply rails, often something like plus and minus 15 V, or a single 5 V supply, and its output transistors need a bit of headroom near each rail to keep operating in their linear region. On a standard bipolar output stage under load, that headroom is commonly one to two volts from each rail. The output simply cannot physically go beyond supply voltage minus that headroom, no matter what the gain equation says should happen.

Work through a concrete case. Build a non-inverting amplifier with a gain of 10 (say Rf = 90 kΩ, Rg = 10 kΩ, giving 1 + 90k/10k = 10) and power it from a plus and minus 15 V supply. Feed it a 2 V input. The ideal equation predicts Vout = 10 x 2 V = 20 V. But with roughly 2 V of headroom needed on each side of a 15 V rail, the largest voltage this op-amp can actually produce is about 13 V. Since the requested 20 V is well beyond the achievable 13 V, the amplifier cannot deliver it: the output saturates, sticking at approximately +13 V instead. If the 2 V input were instead a sine wave swinging between plus and minus 2 V, the output would try to swing between plus and minus 20 V, and every peak beyond about 13 V would get sliced off flat, a distortion called clipping.

Saturation is a large-signal amplitude limit, distinct from the frequency-domain limit of bandwidth and the slope limit of slew rate covered earlier in this chapter sequence, but the three interact in a real circuit. A clipped waveform has sharp corners where the signal suddenly stops rising and goes flat, and reproducing those sharp corners accurately would itself require fast transitions, which can brush up against slew rate limits at the edges of the clipped region.

The design rule that follows is simple to state and easy to check: before trusting a gain calculation, verify that Gain x Vin(max) stays within the supply voltage minus the output stage's headroom. If it doesn't, there are a few ways out: reduce the gain, reduce the expected input amplitude, raise the supply rails if the application allows it, or choose an op-amp built specifically to minimize that lost headroom, the subject of the next chapter.
